questions.q: According to Yijing, how many times did the water-clock bowl sink in one full day and night at Nalanda?
questions.do: Read the paragraph under the water-clock quote in The water clock that ran the day.
questions.a: 32 sinkings. Four hours by day and four by night make eight hours, and each hour had four sinkings.

questions.q: How does the length of one sinking change between midsummer and midwinter at Nalanda?
questions.do: Set Day of the year to 21 June and read Day length and Each sinking. Then set it to 21 December.
questions.a: On 21 June the day is about 13 h 34 m and each daytime sinking is about 51 min. On 21 December the day is about 10 h 26 m and each sinking about 39 min. Daytime hours stretched with the seasons, which is why the hole was sized “according to the time of the year”.

questions.q: What happens to each sinking if you use the Mahabodhi rule instead of Nalanda's?
questions.do: Keep Day of the year at 21 March and read Each sinking and Pin-hole needed. Then click Mahabodhi rule and read them again.
questions.a: Nalanda rule: about 45 min per sinking, with a pin-hole of about 0.91 mm. Mahabodhi rule: 16 sinkings before noon, so about 22 min each, close to a 24-minute ghatika, and a bigger hole of about 1.28 mm so the bowl fills faster.

questions.q: In Dignaga's wheel of reasons, why is a reason that is found everywhere useless as proof?
questions.do: In An idea to try: Dignaga's wheel of reasons, click the box where the reason is Found in all places like the claim and Found in all places unlike it.
questions.a: It is Inconclusive: the reason is everywhere, with or without the claim, so it proves nothing. Smoke works for fire only because it is found with fire and in no place without fire.

questions.q: A popular claim says Nalanda had 10,000 students. What do the eyewitnesses and the modern excavations say?
questions.do: Read the row 10,000 students and 1,510 teachers in the table What the sources say, and what they don't.
questions.a: Verdict: Partly supported. Hui Li gives 10,000, but Xuanzang says “several thousands” and Yijing, there for ten years, says over 3,000. Asher notes the excavated halls cannot hold 10,000, so a modern look at the ruins checks the old number.
